blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = 2x + 5\), \(g(x) = -x + 5\).
blocks.explanation:
Two straight lines: they meet where they have the same x and the same y, i.e. where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find that common point.
Plan: one table with the same x-values for both lines, look for the column where the outputs agree, draw both lines on the same axes, read the crossing, and confirm by algebra.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 2x + 5\) and \(g(x) = -x + 5\), two linear functions.
To find: the point where their graphs cross.
Method: tabulate both functions for the same x-values, plot both lines, and read the common point; at that point \(f(x) = g(x)\).

Make one table for both functions
\[x:\ -2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2\]
\[f(x):\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9\]
\[g(x):\ 7,\ 6,\ 5,\ 4,\ 3\]
Why: using the same x-values lets us compare the two outputs column by column. At \(x = 0\) both outputs are equal.

Draw both lines on the same axes
\(f\): rising line (slope 2) through \((0, 5)\) and \((-\tfrac{5}{2}, 0)\).
\(g\): falling line (slope \(-1\)) through \((0, 5)\) and \((5, 0)\).
The two lines cross at \((0,\ 5)\).
Why: One line rises (slope 2) and the other falls (slope \(-1\)); both have y-intercept 5, so they meet on the y-axis. The crossing point is the only point lying on both lines.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[2x + 5 = -x + 5\]
\[3x = 0\]
\[x = 0\]
\[y = 2(0) + 5 = 5\]
Why: adding \(x\) and subtracting 5 on both sides collects the x-terms on one side.

Check
\[f(0) = 2(0) + 5 = 5\]
\[g(0) = -0 + 5 = 5 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the point must satisfy both equations, because it lies on both lines.

answer_figure.alt: Rising line f(x) = 2x + 5 and falling line g(x) = -x + 5 crossing at (0, 5) on the y-axis.
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (i): both lines and their meeting point (original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = 3x - 2\), \(g(x) = 10 - x\).
blocks.explanation:
Two straight lines: they meet where they have the same x and the same y, i.e. where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find that common point.
Plan: one table with the same x-values for both lines, look for the column where the outputs agree, draw both lines on the same axes, read the crossing, and confirm by algebra.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 3x - 2\) and \(g(x) = 10 - x\), two linear functions.
To find: the point where their graphs cross.
Method: tabulate both functions for the same x-values, plot both lines, and read the common point; at that point \(f(x) = g(x)\).

Make one table for both functions
\[x:\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4\]
\[f(x):\ 1,\ 4,\ 7,\ 10\]
\[g(x):\ 9,\ 8,\ 7,\ 6\]
Why: using the same x-values lets us compare the two outputs column by column. At \(x = 3\) both outputs are equal.

Draw both lines on the same axes
\(f\): rising line (slope 3) through \((0, -2)\) and \((\tfrac{2}{3}, 0)\).
\(g\): falling line (slope \(-1\)) through \((0, 10)\) and \((10, 0)\).
The two lines cross at \((3,\ 7)\).
Why: \(f\) rises steeply and \(g\) falls slowly, so they cross once, to the right of the y-axis. The crossing point is the only point lying on both lines.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[3x - 2 = 10 - x\]
\[3x + x = 10 + 2\]
\[4x = 12\]
\[x = 3\]
\[y = 3(3) - 2 = 7\]
Why: moving \(-x\) to the left and \(-2\) to the right (changing their signs) collects like terms.

Check
\[f(3) = 9 - 2 = 7\]
\[g(3) = 10 - 3 = 7 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the point must satisfy both equations, because it lies on both lines.

answer_figure.alt: Rising line f(x) = 3x - 2 and falling line g(x) = 10 - x crossing at (3, 7).
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (ii): both lines and their meeting point (original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = 2x - 4\), \(g(x) = 3x - 1\).
blocks.explanation:
Two straight lines: they meet where they have the same x and the same y, i.e. where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find that common point.
Plan: one table with the same x-values for both lines, look for the column where the outputs agree, draw both lines on the same axes, read the crossing, and confirm by algebra.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 2x - 4\) and \(g(x) = 3x - 1\), two linear functions.
To find: the point where their graphs cross.
Method: tabulate both functions for the same x-values, plot both lines, and read the common point; at that point \(f(x) = g(x)\).

Make one table for both functions
\[x:\ -4,\ -3,\ -2,\ -1,\ 0\]
\[f(x):\ -12,\ -10,\ -8,\ -6,\ -4\]
\[g(x):\ -13,\ -10,\ -7,\ -4,\ -1\]
Why: using the same x-values lets us compare the two outputs column by column. At \(x = -3\) both outputs are equal.

Draw both lines on the same axes
\(f\): rising line (slope 2) through \((0, -4)\) and \((2, 0)\).
\(g\): steeper rising line (slope 3) through \((0, -1)\) and \((\tfrac{1}{3}, 0)\).
The two lines cross at \((-3,\ -10)\).
Why: Both lines rise but with different slopes (2 and 3), so they are not parallel and cross exactly once; the crossing is far down in the third quadrant, so the y-axis must reach \(-10\). The crossing point is the only point lying on both lines.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[2x - 4 = 3x - 1\]
\[-4 + 1 = 3x - 2x\]
\[x = -3\]
\[y = 2(-3) - 4 = -10\]
Why: subtracting \(2x\) and adding 1 on both sides leaves \(x\) alone.

Check
\[f(-3) = -6 - 4 = -10\]
\[g(-3) = -9 - 1 = -10 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the point must satisfy both equations, because it lies on both lines.

answer_figure.alt: Two rising lines f(x) = 2x - 4 and g(x) = 3x - 1 crossing at (-3, -10) in the third quadrant.
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (iii): both lines and their meeting point (original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = -3x - 4\), \(g(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3\).
blocks.explanation:
Two straight lines: they meet where they have the same x and the same y, i.e. where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find that common point.
Plan: one table with the same x-values for both lines, look for the column where the outputs agree, draw both lines on the same axes, read the crossing, and confirm by algebra.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = -3x - 4\) and \(g(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3\), two linear functions.
To find: the point where their graphs cross.
Method: tabulate both functions for the same x-values, plot both lines, and read the common point; at that point \(f(x) = g(x)\).

Make one table for both functions
\[x:\ -4,\ -2,\ 0,\ 2\]
\[f(x):\ 8,\ 2,\ -4,\ -10\]
\[g(x):\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4\]
Why: using the same x-values lets us compare the two outputs column by column. At \(x = -2\) both outputs are equal.

Draw both lines on the same axes
\(f\): falling line (slope \(-3\)) through \((0, -4)\) and \((-\tfrac{4}{3}, 0)\).
\(g\): gently rising line (slope \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)) through \((0, 3)\) and \((-6, 0)\).
The two lines cross at \((-2,\ 2)\).
Why: One line falls steeply and the other rises gently; they cross in the second quadrant. We used even x-values so that \(\tfrac{1}{2}x\) is a whole number. The crossing point is the only point lying on both lines.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[-3x - 4 = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3\]
\[-6x - 8 = x + 6\]
\[-7x = 14\]
\[x = -2\]
\[y = -3(-2) - 4 = 2\]
Why: multiplying every term by 2 clears the fraction \(\tfrac{1}{2}\); then we collect like terms.

Check
\[f(-2) = 6 - 4 = 2\]
\[g(-2) = -1 + 3 = 2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the point must satisfy both equations, because it lies on both lines.

answer_figure.alt: Falling line f(x) = -3x - 4 and gently rising line g(x) = (1/2)x + 3 crossing at (-2, 2) in the second quadrant.
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (iv): both lines and their meeting point (original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = x - 1\), \(g(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\).
blocks.explanation:
A line and a parabola: they can meet at two points, one point or none. The meeting points are where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find all the meeting points.
Plan: find the parabola's vertex and intercepts, make one table for both graphs around the vertex, draw both on the same axes, read the crossings and confirm with a quadratic equation.
steps:
Given: the line \(f(x) = x - 1\) and the parabola \(g(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\).
To find: all points where the two graphs meet.
Method: sketch the parabola from its vertex and intercepts, tabulate both functions, plot them together and read the crossings; then solve \(f(x) = g(x)\) to confirm.

Study the parabola
\[a = 1,\ b = -4,\ c = 3\]
\[x = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\]
\[g(2) = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1\]
Vertex \((2, -1)\); the parabola opens upwards.
Why: the vertex is the turning point of the parabola, so we choose the table's x-values on both sides of it; \(a > 0\) means the parabola opens upwards.

Find the parabola's intercepts
y-intercept: \(g(0) = 3\), so \((0, 3)\).
\[x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\]
\[(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0\]
x-intercepts: \((1, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\).
Why: intercepts are exact points that are easy to plot and help us draw the curve accurately.

Make one table for both graphs
\[x:\ 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5\]
\[f(x):\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4\]
\[g(x):\ 3,\ 0,\ -1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 8\]
Why: where the two rows have the same value, the graphs share a point. The rows agree at \(x = 1\) (both 0) and at \(x = 4\) (both 3).

Draw both graphs on the same axes
\(f\): rising line (slope 1) through \((0, -1)\) and \((1, 0)\).
\(g\): a U-shaped curve through the table points, symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex.
The graphs cross at \((1,\ 0) \text{ and } (4,\ 3)\).
Why: a line can cut an upward parabola at most twice. One crossing \((1, 0)\) is on the x-axis, where the line passes through an x-intercept of the parabola.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[x - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 3\]
\[x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0\]
\[(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0\]
\[x = 1 \text{ or } x = 4\]
\[f(1) = 0,\quad f(4) = 3\]
Why: bringing every term to one side gives a quadratic equation; its roots are the x-coordinates of the meeting points, and the line gives the y-coordinates.

Check
\[g(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0 = f(1) \;\checkmark\]
\[g(4) = 16 - 16 + 3 = 3\]
\[f(4) = 4 - 1 = 3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: each point must satisfy both equations.

answer_figure.alt: Line f(x) = x - 1 and upward parabola g(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 with vertex (2, -1); they meet at (1, 0) and (4, 3).
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (v): the line, the parabola and their meeting points (original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 2 (vi) Find the point(s) of intersection of the following functions graphically: \(f(x) = 3x + 4\), \(g(x) = x^2 + 2x - 8\).
blocks.explanation:
A line and a parabola: they can meet at two points, one point or none. The meeting points are where \(f(x) = g(x)\).
We must find all the meeting points.
Plan: find the parabola's vertex and intercepts, make one table for both graphs around the vertex, draw both on the same axes, read the crossings and confirm with a quadratic equation.
steps:
Given: the line \(f(x) = 3x + 4\) and the parabola \(g(x) = x^2 + 2x - 8\).
To find: all points where the two graphs meet.
Method: sketch the parabola from its vertex and intercepts, tabulate both functions, plot them together and read the crossings; then solve \(f(x) = g(x)\) to confirm.

Study the parabola
\[a = 1,\ b = 2,\ c = -8\]
\[x = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{2}{2} = -1\]
\[g(-1) = 1 - 2 - 8 = -9\]
Vertex \((-1, -9)\); the parabola opens upwards.
Why: the vertex is the turning point of the parabola, so we choose the table's x-values on both sides of it; \(a > 0\) means the parabola opens upwards.

Find the parabola's intercepts
y-intercept: \(g(0) = -8\), so \((0, -8)\).
\[x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0\]
\[(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0\]
x-intercepts: \((-4, 0)\) and \((2, 0)\).
Why: intercepts are exact points that are easy to plot and help us draw the curve accurately.

Make one table for both graphs
\[x:\ -4,\ -3,\ -2,\ -1,\ 0\]
\[f(x):\ -8,\ -5,\ -2,\ 1,\ 4\]
\[g(x):\ 0,\ -5,\ -8,\ -9,\ -8\]
Why: where the two rows have the same value, the graphs share a point. The rows agree at \(x = -3\) (both \(-5\)). Continuing the table to \(x = 1, 2, 3, 4\) gives \(f: 7, 10, 13, 16\) and \(g: -5, 0, 7, 16\), so they agree again at \(x = 4\) (both 16).

Draw both graphs on the same axes
\(f\): rising line (slope 3) through \((0, 4)\) and \((-\tfrac{4}{3}, 0)\).
\(g\): a U-shaped curve through the table points, symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex.
The graphs cross at \((-3,\ -5) \text{ and } (4,\ 16)\).
Why: a line can cut an upward parabola at most twice. The second crossing is high up at \((4, 16)\), so the y-axis must go up to about 20; a scale of 1 square = 2 units on the y-axis is convenient.

Confirm by algebra (put \(f(x) = g(x)\))
\[x^2 + 2x - 8 = 3x + 4\]
\[x^2 - x - 12 = 0\]
\[(x - 4)(x + 3) = 0\]
\[x = 4 \text{ or } x = -3\]
\[f(4) = 16,\quad f(-3) = -5\]
Why: bringing every term to one side gives a quadratic equation; its roots are the x-coordinates of the meeting points, and the line gives the y-coordinates.

Check
\[g(-3) = 9 - 6 - 8 = -5\]
\[f(-3) = -9 + 4 = -5 \;\checkmark\]
\[g(4) = 16 + 8 - 8 = 16\]
\[f(4) = 12 + 4 = 16 \;\checkmark\]
Why: each point must satisfy both equations.

answer_figure.alt: Line f(x) = 3x + 4 and upward parabola g(x) = x^2 + 2x - 8 with vertex (-1, -9); they meet at (-3, -5) and (4, 16).
answer_figure.caption: Question 2 (vi): the line, the parabola and their meeting points (original drawing)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (book pages 294-295) shows eight graphs, labelled (i) to (viii), for this question, but only six parts are printed. Graphs (i) to (vi) match the printed parts; graphs (vii) and (viii) (a line with a parabola) belong to no printed part and should be ignored.
